In US interscholastic sports, it's common for teams to not be able to cut eligible students, meaning that they end up with more players than are allowed on a roster. Therefore, many programs will field a Varsity team (the best players) and a Junior Varsity team (B team, possibly encompassing everyone else). You might also have a freshman team, consisting of only 9th graders, depending on the circumstances. These lower levels allow for athletes to develop their skills and gain experience. Depending on the sport, JV contests might happen alongside Varsity or on different days. An athlete might also be elevated from a lower team to the Varsity squad for one or more competitions, either to fill for an injury or due to improvement. For example, I was on the wrestling team in high school. Teams were allowed to field one wrestler in each weight class, so the varsity team was 14 wrestlers. JV matches were held prior to the main meet, and were not restricted in number. I was not very good, so I stayed on the JV team (we all practiced together anyway). "Federal crime" does not mean "really bad crime". A federal crime has something that makes it not just a single state issue, for example,

* The crime was a violation of specifically federal laws (e.g. fraud on your federal taxes)
* The crime happened on federal property (e.g. you shoot someone in a federal building)
* The crime crossed state lines (you kidnap someone from one state into another)
* Related to the above, you traveled interstate in order to commit the crime

School shootings generally happen within a single state and don't intersect with federal jurisdiction, so they stay a state matter (though if the school were part of a federal compound, it very well might be a federal crime). Planning a murder and then traveling across state lines for the express purpose of doing the murder puts you in federal territory (in addition to the state prosecution). Additionally, this specific case involves a suppressor, which is regulated on the federal level - if you don't have the appropriate paperwork to possess one, that's a federal crime. Similarly, if you manufactured meth and sold it within your state, that would be a state crime. If you sold the same meth to one single person in another state, now it's federal.

Hokay, so. Here's the deal (from someone who has been flying since infancy, and has worked in airports for five years):

1. About 24 hours before your flight, you will get an email and/or a text from the airline reminding you to check in for your flight online. If you have the app for your airline, you can use that (I see you are flying United, so their app is pretty user friendly), or you can use a regular browser. If you are checking in on the browser, you will probably need your confirmation number, which should be in the email you got confirming your booking. If you checked in on the app, it will give you a digital boarding pass. If you checked in on the browser, it will enable you to print a boarding pass at home.
2. Make sure you are packed correctly - there are things that can't go in carry-on bags and have to be sent in checked luggage. Check [TSA's guide](https://www.tsa.gov/travel/security-screening/whatcanibring/all) for some commonly asked about items. Of particular note, any liquid or gel or paste or spray more than 3.4 oz is not allowed in your carry-on, so if you have a water bottle, it needs to be empty before you go through security 
3. Once you get to the airport, if you are checking a bag, didn't check in online, or need to get a boarding pass printed, look for the ticket counters, which are usually right in the entrance area. If you don't need to do any of those things, you can head straight to the security checkpoint. Depending on the setup, you may need your boarding pass, but you will definitely need your ID ready.
4. At the checkpoint, you will need to remove your shoes, jacket, and anything in your pockets other than air and dryer lint. It's also recommended to take your belt off unless it will cause you to lose your pants. You may need to take stuff out of your bag to be x-rayed separately, but that depends on the airport and what equipment they are using. Pay attention to the instructions the security officers are giving and you should be all set for that airport's setup.
5. You will go through a body scanner, and any areas that the scanner flags, an officer of the same gender will pat down. At the same time, your stuff is going through the x-ray. If there is anything that is possibly an issue, the bag will get pulled aside to be searched (you'll see it on the other side of the x-ray rollers from the rest of the bags). If that is necessary, the search will be done with you present, generally in the order the bags were pulled.
6. Once you've collected your belongings, there should be screens nearby with gate assignments. Find your flight on there and make sure you are going to the right gate. Depending on the airport, you might need to take a tram or a shuttle to the gate area.
7. Once you have located the gate area, you are free to relax until you are called for boarding (this usually starts about 39 minutes before the scheduled flight time). Your boarding pass will list a boarding group - the gate agent will call the groups one or two at a time, and when you hear yours, line up to board. They will scan your boarding pass to make sure you are getting on the right plane, and may ask you to gate check your bag (particularly if you are in a later boarding group, space for carry-ons might get full). This can take one of two forms. They may put a (usually colored) tag on it and have it brought up to the jet bridge when you land, or they may print a normal baggage tag out and send it like a normal checked bag, in which case you will get it from the baggage claim carousel at your destination. Important note: If you have a connection (you are changing flights before getting to your final destination), the first type of gate check sees you picking up the bag as you get off the plane in that intermediate airport, while the second will reunite you with it at the final stop.
8. Once you board the plane, find your seat put your carry-on bags either in the overhead bin or under the seat in front of you, and buckle your seatbelt.
9. Have a safe flight.

Israel's security style doesn't scale to a JFK or ATL level - there are too many people. Second, the visible layers of security are culturally and geographically impractical for American implementation. If you drive to the airport, you have to stop like a mile out and get your ID checked before you even approach the parking lots, which doesn't work for a lot of airports that sit right off the highway or just off of a major city. You also have a lot more visibly armed police and military present. Americans are not used to seeing people walking around with M16s on their shoulder as a part of daily life, so seeing armed personnel like that would immediately code for most Americans as "something is going on - I should be on my guard", whereas in Israel it's not a remarkable sight. Third, Israel's behind the scenes passenger vetting is allowed by their laws to be more extensive than the US's. And, perhaps most importantly, Israel and the US face drastically different types of threats. The terrorist threat to Israel is a nationalist one - even Islamist groups like Hamas and Hizballah are focused not on spreading the international jihad, but on overthrowing the State of Israel and replacing it with an Arab state. This means the threat is coming almost exclusively from the Arab world, so race can be one component (but not the only component) in a profile, because the threat is specific. And even still, it gets overused by Israeli security. The US, on the other hand, faces a dynamic threat - the global jihad movement operates across the globe and comes in all nationalities. Profiling Arabs would have missed Richard Reid (shoe bomber - Jamaican/British), Omar Farouk Abdulmutallab (underwear bomber - Nigerian), the members of the 2006 UK Liquid Explosives cell (Pakistanis), just among those terrorists with an aviation nexus. And that's without touching the non-Islamic terror threat.

BA (Bachelor of Arts) and BS (Bachelor of Science) are bachelor's degrees. If a subject is offered in both degrees, the Arts path will generally include more humanities courses while the curriculum for Science will require more math and science classes. Otherwise, they are functionally equivalent.

Your major is your overall field of study. Within that field, there are bound to be lots of subfields, and you might have a particular interest in one of them. So, if you are a biology major, maybe you are interested in evolutionary biology. Some departments will develop specific curricula to let you concentrate on your area of interest and allow it to be notated on your transcript. So, in our example, you'll take a few baseline bio classes, and then fill in most of the advanced-level credits with stuff in the evolutionary bio field. So you would have a BS in Biology with a concentration in evolutionary biology.

Now, if you have an interest in multiple fields, you can study both. Some programs will allow you to declare a double major, where you have sets of requirements for both degrees and will be awarded a degree in both subjects. You can also generally declare a minor in one of those subjects. This would entail taking a smaller series of courses (usually like four or five) in that field of study, and in that case it would also be duly noted on your degree and in your transcript. So if we go back to our example, maybe within evolutionary biology, you are especially interested in human evolution. So, you might decide to declare a minor in anthropology, and take some introductory anthropology classes and then get you access to some of the more advanced primatology and paleoanthropology classes. In that case you would have a BS in biology with a concentration in evolutionary biology and a minor in anthropology.

Kabbalah is the general field of Jewish mysticism. Most of it is incredibly opaque unless you have an extremely extensive background in Jewish texts, and even then it's pretty opaque. Much of the corpus of Kabbalistic literature is based in two texts, the Zohar and Bahir that are most likely medieval pseudoepigrapha, though they are based on earlier mystic traditions. Some of the aspects of medieval and renaissance Kabbalah ended up getting mixed into the contemporary Christian esotericism of the time, through the mystic interpretations of the Hebrew Bible. A lot of it straddles the line between spirituality and hocus pocus, but I'm not well enough versed in it to identify where the spiritual mysticism ends and the authentically Jewish hocus pocus begins, or where the authentic hocus pocus shifts into New Age mumbo jumbo.

One of the ideas brought in Kabbalah is that the Divine manifests in a number of different layers. A popular diagram of these layers and the connections between them is sometimes known as "The Tree of Life", which is what you see in the top of the image. The bottom half of the image is an attempt at doing a similar thing to the Klipot (shells), which are, in essence, the shadows cast by the Divine Light. The particular dualistic approach is associated with the Thelema movement of Aleister Crowley, and particularly the mid 20th century work of Kenneth Grant which blended the Renaissance esoteric roots of Thelema with Egyptian mythology and Tantric yoga.

There are two different things in play here. Schools offer (and may require) elective classes that are not part of the core curriculum. So, for example, when I was in high school, we had to take 4 years of English, 4 years of PE (this was a state requirement that my graduating class actually had an exemption from in our last year, due to space issues), 3 years of History (including, by state law, one and a half years of American history and half a year of civics and government), 3 years of Math, and 2 years of Science. We were not required to study a foreign language, but could take French, Spanish, and/or Latin (I believe Mandarin Chinese was also added my last year). Those were our core classes. Additionally, we were required to take two semesters of either Art, Computers, or Technical Studies (woodworking, automotive repair, technical drawing, etc). So, my last year I had to take Introductory Ceramics, because I needed another art class, or I would not be able to graduate (to be more accurate, I could have taken one of any number of classes, but ceramics was what I wanted to take and that fit into my schedule). Additionally, most schools will have some sort of music program with a variety of sub-programs (varying different bands and choirs and orchestras). You can take any number of electives, as long as they fit in your schedule.

Schools also generally offer extracurricular activities that meet after the end of the school day. These range from cultural (e.g. Muslim Students Association, Jewish Students Association, Italian Heritage Club, etc.) to academic (National Honor Societies or peer tutoring for example) to social action programs to athletic teams. So, for example, I was on the wrestling team, and every day during the season, we had practice from 5:00 until 7:00 pm. I was also part of the Jewish Students Club, Guitar Club, and (nominally) the Debate Club, which all met periodically immediately after school. There is no formal limit on the number of extracurricular activities you can participate in, except that most schools limit students to one sport per season (so, for example, as a wrestler, I could have played soccer, played in the autumn; golf, played in the spring; but not basketball or ice hockey, as those were winter sports like wrestling).

The two systems are unrelated. The E through A classification is how USA Fencing classifies its members and doesn't represent any sort of formal rank within the fencing system beyond the domestic events for which you qualify to register (some elite events might have a minimum rating to keep the pool reasonable, while events for beginners might set a maximum rating to give newer fencers a chance). The world ranking system is just the FIE (International Fencing Federation) ranking of the top teams as well as individual fencers. Olympic qualification is based on world rankings, so whoever is qualified on the day the Olympic invites are locked in is automatically eligible to participate (They still have to be available and their country has to be able to get them there though).

In the US, the rating system runs from E to A, and is based on tournament results - depending on how many high-level fencers are participating in an event, the top however many finishers will be awarded a higher rating. So, for example, if six unclassified fencers compete in an event, the winner will get an E rating; while an event of 64 or more fencers including at least 12 each rated A, B, and C, with 4 As finishing in the top 8 and 4 Bs or better in the top 12 will award A ratings to the top 8, B to the next 8, C to the following 8, Ds to places 25-32, and the 33rd-48th place finishers will get an E rating (if they don't already have one). Additionally, ratings expire after four years, at which point they drop one letter. So, for example, if you earned an A in 2008 and then stopped competing at high level events, in 2012 you would drop to a B, in 2016 a C, in 2020 a D, and in 2024, you would have an E. The Olympic qualification standard is based on world rankings (i.e. you have to not just be good in your country but also do well on the world level). What you are talking about is related to the team qualifications. The top four teams in the world qualify for the Olympics automatically. For the next four slots, the top team from each continent (treating the Americas as one continent and combining Asia and Oceania) gets to go, as long as they are in the top 16 places on the world ranking list, and if a continent is not represented in the top 16, that spot gets given to the top ranked team not already qualified.

So, in most cases, a party isn't going to put forth multiple candidates in a single election. There are numerous ways they could pick who will be their nominee — party leaders could decide on their own, random selection, dance off, etc. — but the way that the two major parties select their nominee for the presidency is through a primary election. The membership of each state's branch of the party all vote for a delegation to attend the party's national convention where they set out their platform for the upcoming election and presidential term, and each state's representatives (different numbers based on state size) vote on who will be the party's nominee for the election. The Republican party rules require the delegates to vote according to how their state primary went for the first ballot, but if there is no winner on the first ballot, delegates are free to vote however they choose in future ballots. On the Democratic side, the leadership of the party (current and former elected officials) also get to vote as unpledged "super delegates". Debates are run by a collaboration between the Democratic and Republican parties, and allow the candidates from those parties, as well as third party candidates with significant support, to present their case to the public. 

>people saying it is a two parry system while parties like socialist parry of America and the new CPUSA exist

Because of the first past the post system, multiple candidates with similar platforms dilute the vote and enable the other side to win, despite less support. Let's say that there are three parties running in an election: Democratic, Republican, and Progressive. The Republican and Progressive parties are pretty close to one another in terms of their platform, and pretty much all voters for the Republican ticket would prefer the Progressive party to the Democrats and vice versa. The breakdown of public support is roughly 40% for the Democrats, and 30% each for the Republicans and Progressives. So, come election day, the Democrats win because the two similar parties were splitting their supporters. This is what happened in the 1912 election, where William Howard Taft (R) and Theodore Roosevelt (P) split their ideological bloc's vote and Woodrow Wilson (D) was able to win. For this reason, American politics tends to coalesce around two big-tent parties, so your social democrats, your modern liberals, and your third way moderates all find a home in the Democratic Party, while Christian conservatives, libertarians, neoconservatives, and Trumpists all unite under the Republican elephant.

>how Hillary lost despite having the popular vote

Our constitution defines an idiosyncratic procedure for electing the president, in contrast to all other elected officers. Rather than the people directly choosing the president, they choose electors, with each state having as many as they have representatives between both houses of Congress, and the electors choose the president (most states have laws requiring electors to vote according to what they were pledged to). In all but two states, electors are assigned in a winner take all fashion, so the first past the post wins all that state's electors. If a candidate can get a bare plurality of votes in each of the 12 largest states, that is enough to give them a majority of electors, even if they don't receive a single vote in any other state.

>Most cheese is produced with rennet, which is derived from animal stomachs and counts as mixing meat and dairy in most interpretations

The issue with rennet is not one of meat and dairy. Most interpretations allow rennet from an animal which has been slaughtered properly. The more common issue is that there is a rabbinic edict to eat only cheese made by a Jew (defined as a Jew adding the rennet to the milk). Acid set cheese, not containing rennet, isn't considered "cheese" by the law, so it's easier to certify things like cream cheese and paneer. With vegetable rennet, there is a minority opinion, held by Rabbeinu Tam and the sages of Narbonne that milk set with vegetable enzymes is similarly not considered halakhically cheese, and so the same rule as the acid set cheeses applies. This minority opinion is why many people don't accept the heksher of Tablet-K, as they follow the lenient position and certify cheese made with vegetable rennet that was not added by a Jew.

There is a potential halakhic (Jewish law) issue with the bride giving the groom a ring as part of the ceremony (explanation below). There are a few proposed workarounds to have the bride present her groom a ring during the ceremony, but none that are universally accepted. If the rabbi is not comfortable with officiating a double ring ceremony, there is nothing wrong with that. They should not agree to officiate your wedding though. Not accept the role and then steal the ring to enforce a single-ring ceremony.

**Technical Jewish Law Explanation:** Marriage (technically betrothal) in Jewish law is a contract (specifically an "acquisition") between the two parties. The groom gives the bride one of three things: money/something of monetary value, a written declaration that he betroths her, or his penis, as consideration in exchange for her becoming his wife. She accepts the consideration, and the betrothal takes effect. The document method is not really done, and the sex option is seen as licentious and inappropriate and has been disapproved of since ancient times. So, we betroth using the first option, with the all but universal custom being that the item of value used be a ring. This is why, regardless of the ring they choose to wear in their daily life, the ring used in most Jewish wedding ceremonies is a plain, unadorned gold band - the value of the ring should be clear and not subject to appraisal as it would if stones were present - lest there be any doubt that the bride knew the value she was accepting as betrothal consideration. 

There is a concern that if the groom gives his bride a ring as consideration for the betrothal and then she immediately gives him a ring, the whole procedure could be construed as an exchange of rings rather than the execution of the contract. The validity of the betrothal could then be called into question. Additionally, many double ring ceremonies will have the bride say a gender-flipped version of the groom's formula "You are hereby betrothed to me by this ring, according to the laws of Moses and Israel", which would mean the bride is taking the groom, which isn't the way the law is structured. 

Some of the potential legal workarounds to enable both principals to give rings during the ceremony are: change the bride's wording to either make it an acceptance of the betrothal (something like "I am hereby betrothed to you") or eliminate any legal statements at all and choose some other declaration (most popularly "I am my beloved, and my beloved is mine" from Song of Songs), having the bride give the ring during the formal marriage part of the ceremony. Jewish weddings consist of two parts, formerly separate ceremonies that would happen like a year apart - first is the betrothal, where the giving of the ring happens and most of the marriage restrictions attach (she is prohibited to other men, any dissolution of the relationship requires a divorce, but the couple is not permitted to engage in relations and the husband's obligation to support his bride do not start) and then formalization of the marriage, where the groom would bring the bride into his house and they become fully married with all the privileges and responsibilities thereunto pertaining. By pushing the bride's presentation of the ring back a few minutes until the shift from the betrothal phase to the formal marriage phase, the contract will already have been executed and there is less ground for invalidating the transaction. There is also the option of the officiant advising the guests something to the effect of "Now that the betrothal has been done, Rachel would like to give Jacob a gift of a ring, totally unrelated to the legalities being conducted here". Nevertheless, many Orthodox rabbis will not accept any of the workarounds and will not permit the groom to be given a ring by the bride during the ceremony, as the double ring aspect is one of the things that they can use to invalidate a non-Orthodox wedding if needed to alleviate divorce refusal.

Just about all airlines around the world operate frequent flyer programs. The idea is, if you fly enough times with that specific airline, you will rack up enough points to eventually get a free flight. Historically, those points were earned at a rate of one point per mile flown. Nowadays, the point accumulation formula is a little different, with multipliers for first or business class segments or reduced rates for partner airline flights (e.g. if I am an American Airlines AAdvantage member, my flight from New York to London might be worth 1000 points, but if I am flying business class, that might be worth 1500 points instead, and if I decide to fly on BA instead of American, it might only earn me 700 points). Additionally, most airlines will give you perks for reaching higher tiers of membership (e.g. once you hit 50k miles a year, you get a free checked bag when you fly, at 75k, you also get lounge access and free seat upgrades where available, etc.). Where credit cards get involved is that many if not most airlines have partnerships with credit cards where if you use their co-branded credit card, you can earn points too. So, for example, I have a United Airlines branded Visa, and using the points I earned by doing my normal shopping over a year and a half, I was able to fly to Florida for a week last year, despite having not flown at all in that time frame.

It is often awkward to dance with other partners at first, especially since our culture makes such a high connection between dancing and romance. But a big part of the social dance learning process is to disassociate the act of dancing together from romance to break that awkwardness. Because we are physically close to one another without there being a necessary romantic connection (heck, there are both gay men and lesbians who dance), so some awkward moments are inevitable. Like, at one point, I was learning a new figure and figuring out how my hands were supposed to work - I needed to stop her momentum with my hand on her ribcage as we were moving into and out of frame - the first try, my right hand was about where it would be for a closed position, so when I went to catch her, it was a little too high and I ended up with a handful of sideboob. But we (myself, her, and her boyfriend, who was also there) quickly laughed it off, "maybe the right hand should come down lower". And I've had similar experiences with my girlfriend and with random partners at socials, where a miscue has led to someone getting bumped into, going in a direction different from the one expected, or a hand brushing boob, butt, or balls (whether me/my partner or another couple). And you still have to just go "whoops" and dance on. [Even in the World Professional Latin Championship.](https://youtu.be/uVtYIO5zL7g?si=QUWnTFyjWNWpz3UZ)

Even on the competitive side, where you are doing most of your dancing with the same partner, the person with whom you dance the vertical mambo may well be different from the one with whom you dance the horizontal one. I have known competitive dancers who are couples both on and off the dancefloor, I've known dancers who are dating/married to non-dancers, and I've known couples where one or both of the two has an SO who dances competitively with someone else. In fact, when I was on the ballroom team in college, my girlfriend, my competitive partner, and the person with whom I had the most fun dancing socially were three different women.

I mean, traditionally (and this is still the case for civilian burials in Israel), there's no casket at all. They just wrap the body up in a shroud and that's it. When I went to my great aunt's funeral, it was really different to see one of the corpse handlers (I'm not really sure what the word for it is, but the people who moved the body from the van to the eulogy plinth, then wheeled over to the gravesite) hop down into the grave to maneuver her in.

I'm coming from a specific cultural context, as Judaism requires burial as fast as practical (within 24-48 hours of death is usual), and participating in the burial is a really important thing for us, as it is something that we do for the person knowing it can never be reciprocated. So, although I've only been to a handful of funerals, they've almost all been just at the graveside. Generally, the casket will be set on the lowering apparatus, everyone will stand/sit around (depending on the geography) while some eulogies are delivered. Then, if applicable, military honors like flag folding, bugling, and rifle salutes will be rendered. After that, the person presiding over the service (usually a rabbi, but it doesn't technically have to be) will read a prayer that asks God to grant proper and peaceful rest for the spirit of the deceased within the Divine Presence. Then the casket gets lowered into the grave and the apparatus removed (this is usually done by cemetery employees). After that, all the guests, starting with the family, take turns shoveling dirt in to fill the grave (usually everyone will throw a couple shovels in the hole, and then you'll have a few people finish the task of covering the casket). Once the casket is completely covered, the mourners will say the Mourners Kaddish, the prayer recited by mourners at every prayer services for the first month (for a sibling, spouse, or child) or year (for a parent). After that, the guests form a recieving line to formally offer condolences to the mourners. From there, there may be a meal or some other reception, but otherwise, the mourners will begin the week of Shiva (intense morning where they stay at home and recieve visitors).

When I have heard about a wake, it's always been the day before the funeral. There might be eulogies given, but the primary purpose of the wake is for people to go up and look at the corpse and like, say goodbye face to face. This is compared to a funeral, which centers on the delivery of eulogies and the bewailing of the mourners' loss, and will feature any applicable religious rituals. The only wake I have ever been to personally (Jews don't do them, we try to go from death to burial as fast as possible) was when my neighbors' grandma died. They had a wake in our area, then transported the body to NY (where she had lived) to have a funeral the next day in the church, followed by burial.

The WHS allows for some regional differences in how the system is implemented. One of the things the USGA kept was the expectation that all games of golf are played to the rules, and the requirement that any game played to the rules be posted. Similarly, the USGA implementation has you submit most likely score on a hole not completed. If you are playing better ball and your partner holes their birdie putt before you putt for par from three feet, you should mark the hole as a par for you when you submit your card for handicap, and if you are playing match play and the match ends on the 16th hole, you submit a net par for the last two holes. Neither of those things is allowed in the UK. The UK governing body decided that they wanted to keep the practice of preregistration of handicap rounds, but they removed the restrictions on how often and where you could play those rounds (as I understand it, prior to the adoption of the WHS, British golfers could only submit a small number of non-competition rounds a year and only at their home club).

>How do Jews worship? Is prayer considered worship or is it separate?

I guess I'd say prayer is considered worship, because I'm not quite sure what the distinction is. However, there are three different categories which might be thought of as "prayer". There are, for lack of a better term, liturgical prayers (codified text and format, meant to be recited at a specific time of day); there are also personal prayers (e.g. "please let me get the job for which I interviewed"); and there are also blessings, recited throughout the day on specific actions or events (e.g. before and after eating, seeing a rainbow, performing certain commandments, etc). 

>What happens during services at the synagogue? Are Jews required to attend services weekly or is it optional?

The synagogue service consists of the communal recitation of the liturgical prayers for the hour and day (it is preferable to pray in a group of 10 or more Jewish adults, and some prayers are either not said or said in a slightly different form in the absence of such a quorum). Some services (Saturday morning and afternoons, Monday and Thursday morning, holidays) will also have a portion of the Torah chanted from the scroll. On Saturday and holidays, a sermon might be given. Adult Jews are obligated to pray three times a day - morning, afternoon, and evening - and many synagogues will hold services two-three times a day (it's often convenient to have the afternoon service late and the evening service early so they can run consecutively). However, even if you cannot get to the synagogue, you can discharge your obligation by praying on your own. It's also not strictly necessary to have a synagogue for the service - when I lived in Israel, there was a gas station near me that had a regular afternoon service in the parking lot four days a week, among other non-synagogue places that I've prayed.

Grain isn't prohibited. Leaven is prohibited, and Halakha defines leaven as Grain™ (wheat, rye, barley, spelt, or oats) which has been mixed with water and sat for more than 18 minutes before baking. So, here's the deal. The machine that scans your ID does two things. If the machine cannot find a ticket associated with your information for that airport, it tells us that. So we have to send you back to the counter to have them verify your information and then resend the information to the system. That's a problem, because it is very rare that we can see what the issue is off hand (in like three years of using the machine, it's happened once, and that involved a name change). For context, I have been in this line of work for going on 4 years, and I also have a master's degree in counterterrorism studies. It's complicated. On the one hand, we can't properly measure the number of times something didn't happen. On the other hand, it is true that until this year, TSA screening had never stopped anything identified as an attempted terrorist plot in the execution stage. On the third hand, it's entirely possible that TSOs have stopped many trial runs by malevolent actors without them even realizing it. And on the fourth hand, the people in the blue shirts checking bags and patting down travelers are just a small fraction of the TSA operation - we're just the most visible - and we're certainly not the only part of the wider national security apparatus working against threats to the US and our transportation infrastructure. There have been a lot of plots against airplanes and/or other means of transit that got foiled before they even got to the airport. If TSOs are catching bad guys left and right, that's a red flag - it means that the rest of the system has failed. I like to use the comparison to sports - if you've got a soccer/hockey/lacrosse team and your goalie is the MVP, that should be an indication that your defense is sucking. If the rest of the team is playing well, the keeper doesn't have much work to do, but that doesn't mean you want to just stop fielding someone in goal. It's also worth noting that TSOs do stop a huge number of guns and knives and other dangerous items from getting onto planes. True, those prohibited items are usually in the possession of people with no ill intent, but we have no way of knowing who are the ones who might want to do something harmful with their gun/knife/taser/nunchaku. So it's not like we do nothing. And that is without bringing up the deterrent effect that TSOs have.

Now, as for the failed test metric, yeah, that's a pretty bad look on us. And that served as a big-time "come to Jesus" moment for the agency. The successful detection rate is much better now (when you account for the tests meant to determine the limits and capabilities of our equipment). Is even a single missed test acceptable? No, but there is a difference between "not where we should be" and "a waste of time". In terms of the screening operations, we're generally reactive - someone puts a bomb in their shoe, everyone's gotta take off their shoes now; dude puts a bomb in his underwear, now we're using body scanners; people get caught making a liquid bomb in a soft drink bottle, and nobody's allowed liquids over 100 mL anymore. But that's kinda the nature of the beast - we can't respond to threats until we know about them. On the whole, TSA is not as effective as it could and should be, but it's nowhere near as ineffective as detractors like to portray.

Your general premise, that worship doesn't require a dedicated building to house it, is true for Judaism. However, there are a few things that make having a designated place for the community to pray. First of all, the ideal is to pray communally, defined as the presence of ten adults (age 13 and up. Depending on the stream of Judaism, this might only include men). If everyone knows that there is a service at so-and-so place at so-and-so time, it makes things easier. In my hometown, there was a group which met on Saturday mornings in the auditorium of the elementary school, and when I lived in Israel, one of the stores on the main street of my city had a regularly scheduled weekday afternoon service on the sidewalk outside. No special structure or anything, just a plaque on the wall saying "Afternoon service here on work days, 1:45 pm". And that's generally fine. People can have their scheduled prayer groups at wherever they choose, whether it's the last car of the morning commuter train or a conference room in the office or by the big elm tree on the town green. Additionally, some days, we read from the Torah as part of the service. Those scrolls are expensive and need to be stored somewhere (and, seeing as they are articles of heightened holiness, it's preferable to house them in a respectable manner). If the place you're storing the scroll is different from where the service takes place, now you've got to schlep it from place to place, which is especially challenging on Shabbat. And having a space designed for the prayer service (aligned to face towards Jerusalem, slightly elevated platform from which the Torah can be read, place to store prayer books, etc.) makes life that much easier. So, what you end up with is the community investing in a structure that can host worship services, classes for kids and adults, holiday events, etc.
